title: 5. It happened at Griboyedov’s
paragraphs: The old two-story cream-colored house stood on the Boulevard Ring, at the back of a sickly garden separated from the sidewalk of the Ring by a wrought-iron railing. The small forecourt in front of the house was asphalted, and in wintertime a snowdrift with a shovel stuck in it towered there, while in summertime it turned into the most magnificent section of the summer restaurant, under a canvas awning.

The house was called “Griboyedov House” on the grounds that it had supposedly once belonged to an aunt of the writer Alexander Sergeyevich Griboyedov. Well, whether it belonged to her or not, we do not know for sure. One even recalls that, it seems, Griboyedov never had any such house-owning aunt... Still, that is what the house was called. What is more, a certain Moscow liar used to tell how, on the second floor, in the round hall with columns, the famous writer had supposedly read passages from Woe from Wit to this very aunt as she reclined on a sofa. But then, the devil knows, maybe he did read them; that is not important!
What is important is that at present this house belonged to that same Massolit which had been headed by the unfortunate Mikhail Alexandrovich Berlioz until his appearance at Patriarch’s Ponds.

Thanks to the members of Massolit, nobody called the house “Griboyedov House”; everybody simply said “Griboyedov’s”: “I spent two hours elbowing my way around at Griboyedov’s yesterday.” “And how did it go?” “I wangled a month in Yalta.” “Good for you!” Or: “Go and see Berlioz, he’s receiving at Griboyedov’s today from four to five...” and so on.

Massolit had installed itself at Griboyedov’s in a way that could not have been better or cozier. Anyone entering Griboyedov’s was first of all made acquainted, willy-nilly, with the notices of various sports clubs and with group and individual photographs of the members of Massolit, with which (photographs) the walls of the staircase leading to the second floor were hung.
On the door of the very first room on this upper floor a large sign could be seen, “Fishing and Dacha Section,” and next to it was a picture of a carp caught on a hook.
On the door of room No. 2 something not entirely comprehensible was written: “One-Day Creative Trip Vouchers. Apply to M. V. Podlozhnaya.”

The next door bore a brief but by now altogether incomprehensible sign: “Perelygino.” After that the chance visitor to Griboyedov’s would find his eyes darting about from the signs that dotted the aunt’s walnut doors: “Waiting List for Paper, See Poklevkina,” “Cash Desk. Personal Accounts of Sketch Writers”...
Cutting through an extremely long queue that began downstairs at the doorman’s lodge, one could see a sign on a door that people were storming every second: “Housing Question.”

Past the housing question there opened up a luxurious poster showing a cliff, along whose crest rode a horseman in a felt cloak with a rifle on his shoulder. Lower down, palm trees and a balcony; on the balcony, a seated young man with a forelock, gazing somewhere on high with very, very lively eyes and holding a fountain pen in his hand. The caption: “Full-Length Creative Leaves from Two Weeks (Short Story or Novella) to One Year (Novel, Trilogy). Yalta, Suuk-Su, Borovoye, Tsikhidziri, Makhindzhauri, Leningrad (Winter Palace).” There was a queue at this door too, but not an excessive one, some hundred and fifty people.

Then came, following the whimsical bends, rises and descents of the Griboyedov house, “Massolit Board,” “Cash Desks Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5,” “Editorial Board,” “Chairman of Massolit,” “Billiard Room,” various auxiliary offices and, finally, that same hall with the colonnade where the aunt had relished the comedy of her genius nephew.

Every visitor, provided of course that he was not a complete dimwit, on getting into Griboyedov’s grasped at once how good life was for the lucky members of Massolit, and black envy immediately began to torment him. And immediately he would address bitter reproaches to heaven for not having endowed him at birth with literary talent, without which, naturally, there was no dreaming of acquiring a Massolit membership card—brown, smelling of expensive leather, with a wide gold border—a card known to all Moscow.

Who will say a word in defense of envy? It is a feeling of a rotten sort, but still, one must put oneself in the visitor’s position. For what he had seen on the upper floor was not everything, and far from everything. The entire ground floor of the aunt’s house was taken up by a restaurant, and what a restaurant! In all fairness it was considered the very best in Moscow. And not only because it was housed in two large halls with vaulted ceilings painted with lilac horses with Assyrian manes, not only because on every little table stood a lamp draped with a shawl, not only because it could not be entered by the first person who came in off the street, but also because in the quality of its provisions Griboyedov’s beat any restaurant in Moscow hollow, and these provisions were served at the most reasonable, by no means burdensome prices.
Hence there is nothing surprising in such a conversation as, for instance, the one the author of these most truthful lines once overheard by the wrought-iron railing of Griboyedov’s:
“Where are you having supper tonight, Amvrosy?”
“What a question, here of course, my dear Foka! Archibald Archibaldovich whispered to me today that there will be individual portions of zander au naturel. A virtuoso little item!”
“You know how to live, Amvrosy!” sighed Foka, skinny, neglected, with a carbuncle on his neck, to the red-lipped giant, golden-haired and plump-cheeked Amvrosy the poet.

“I have no special knack at all,” Amvrosy objected, “just an ordinary desire to live like a human being. You mean to say, Foka, that one can come across zander at the Coliseum too. But at the Coliseum a portion of zander costs thirteen roubles fifteen kopecks, and here—five fifty! Besides, at the Coliseum the zander is three days old, and besides that, you have no guarantee that you won’t get a bunch of grapes in the mug at the Coliseum from the first young man who bursts in off Teatralny Passage. No, I am categorically against the Coliseum!” the gastronome Amvrosy thundered for the whole boulevard to hear. “Don’t try to persuade me, Foka!”
“I’m not trying to persuade you, Amvrosy,” Foka squeaked. “One can have supper at home.”

“Your humble servant,” trumpeted Amvrosy. “I can just picture your wife trying to knock together individual portions of zander au naturel in a little saucepan in the communal kitchen of your building! Hee-hee-hee!.. Au revoir, Foka!” And, humming, Amvrosy headed for the veranda under the awning.

Oh-ho-ho... Yes, it was, it was!.. Old Muscovites remember the famous Griboyedov’s! What is boiled zander in portions! Cheap stuff, my dear Amvrosy! But sterlet, sterlet in a silvery saucepan, sterlet in pieces layered with crayfish tails and fresh caviar? And eggs cocotte with mushroom purée in little cups? And didn’t you like the little fillets of thrush? With truffles? Quails à la génoise? Nine and a half roubles! And the jazz, and the courteous service! And in July, when the whole family is at the dacha and urgent literary business keeps you in town—on the veranda, in the shade of the climbing vine, in a golden spot on the cleanest of tablecloths, a little plate of soupe printanière? Remember, Amvrosy? But why ask! I can see by your lips that you remember. What are your whitefish, your zander! What about great snipe, jack snipe, common snipe, woodcock in season, quails, sandpipers? Narzan fizzing in the throat?! But enough, you are getting distracted, reader! Follow me!..

At half past ten on the evening when Berlioz perished at Patriarch’s, only one room was lit upstairs at Griboyedov’s, and in it twelve writers were languishing, who had gathered for the meeting and were waiting for Mikhail Alexandrovich.

Those sitting on chairs, and on tables, and even on the two windowsills in the Massolit board room were suffering seriously from the stuffiness. Not a single fresh current of air came in through the open windows. Moscow was giving off the heat stored up during the day in its asphalt, and it was clear that the night would bring no relief. There was a smell of onions from the basement of the aunt’s house, where the restaurant kitchen was working, and everybody was thirsty, everybody was nervous and cross.

The fiction writer Beskudnikov—a quiet, decently dressed man with attentive and at the same time elusive eyes—took out his watch. The hand was creeping toward eleven. Beskudnikov tapped the dial with his finger and showed it to his neighbor, the poet Dvubratsky, who was sitting on the table and, out of boredom, swinging his feet, shod in yellow shoes with rubber soles.
“Well, really,” grumbled Dvubratsky.

“The lad must have got stuck on the Klyazma,” responded in a thick voice Nastasya Lukinishna Nepremenova, a Moscow merchant’s orphan who had become a writer and composed naval battle stories under the pen name “Navigator Georges.”

“Excuse me!” the author of popular sketches, Zagrivov, spoke up boldly. “I’d enjoy drinking a little tea on a balcony myself right now, instead of stewing in here. The meeting was set for ten, wasn’t it?”

“And it’s lovely on the Klyazma now,” Navigator Georges egged on those present, knowing that the writers’ dacha settlement of Perelygino on the Klyazma was everybody’s sore spot. “The nightingales must be singing by now. I always somehow work better out of town, especially in spring.”

“This is the third year I’ve been paying in my money to send my wife, who has Basedow’s disease, to this paradise, but there’s nothing to be seen on the horizon,” the short-story writer Ieronim Poprikhin said venomously and bitterly.
“That’s a matter of luck,” the critic Ababkov droned from the windowsill.
Joy lit up in Navigator Georges’s little eyes, and she said, softening her contralto:
“We mustn’t envy, comrades. There are only twenty-two dachas, and only seven more are being built, and there are three thousand of us in Massolit.”
“Three thousand one hundred and eleven,” someone put in from a corner.
“So you see,” the Navigator went on, “what can be done? Naturally, the dachas went to the most talented among us...”
“The generals!” Glukharev the screenwriter cut straight into the squabble.
Beskudnikov, with an artificial yawn, went out of the room.
“Five rooms all to himself in Perelygino,” Glukharev said after him.
“Lavrovich has six all to himself,” cried Deniskin, “and the dining room’s paneled in oak!”
“Eh, that’s not the point right now,” droned Ababkov, “the point is that it’s half past eleven.”

A hubbub began; something like a mutiny was brewing. They started telephoning the hated Perelygino, got the wrong dacha, Lavrovich’s, learned that Lavrovich had gone to the river, and were thoroughly upset by it. At random they called the Commission for Belles-Lettres on extension No. 930 and, of course, found no one there.
“He might have telephoned!” shouted Deniskin, Glukharev and Kvant.

Ah, they shouted in vain: Mikhail Alexandrovich could not telephone anywhere. Far, far from Griboyedov’s, in an enormous hall lit by thousand-candlepower lamps, on three zinc tables lay what until recently had been Mikhail Alexandrovich.

On the first, the naked body, caked with dried blood, with a broken arm and a crushed rib cage; on the second, the head, its front teeth knocked out, its clouded eyes open and unafraid of the harshest light; and on the third, a heap of stiffened rags.

Beside the headless body stood a professor of forensic medicine, a pathologist and his prosector, representatives of the investigation, and Mikhail Alexandrovich Berlioz’s deputy in Massolit, the writer Zheldybin, who had been summoned by telephone from the bedside of his sick wife.

A car had called for Zheldybin and first of all, together with the investigators, taken him (this was around midnight) to the dead man’s apartment, where his papers were sealed, and only then did they all go to the morgue.

And now those standing by the remains of the deceased were conferring on what would be best: to sew the severed head back onto the neck, or to lay the body out in the hall at Griboyedov’s, simply covering the dead man up to the chin with a black cloth?

Yes, Mikhail Alexandrovich could not telephone anywhere, and Deniskin, Glukharev and Kvant, along with Beskudnikov, were quite pointlessly indignant and shouting. At exactly midnight all twelve writers left the upper floor and went down to the restaurant. Here again they inwardly cursed Mikhail Alexandrovich: all the tables on the veranda, naturally, had already been taken, and they had to stay and have supper in those beautiful but stuffy halls.

And at exactly midnight in the first of them something crashed, rang out, showered down, leaped. And at once a thin male voice cried out desperately to the music: “Hallelujah!!” It was the famous Griboyedov jazz band striking up. Faces covered with perspiration seemed to light up, the horses painted on the ceiling seemed to come to life, the lamps seemed to give more light, and suddenly, as if breaking loose from a chain, both halls broke into dance, and after them the veranda broke into dance too.

Glukharev started dancing with the poetess Tamara Polumesyats, Kvant started dancing, Zhukopov the novelist started dancing with some film actress in a yellow dress. Dancing were: Dragunsky, Cherdakchi, little Deniskin with the gigantic Navigator Georges, the beautiful architect Semeikina-Gall was dancing, gripped tight by a stranger in white burlap trousers. Dancing were the regulars and invited guests, Muscovites and out-of-towners, the writer Johann from Kronstadt, a certain Vitya Kuftik from Rostov, a director, it seems, with a lilac lichen covering his whole cheek; dancing were the most prominent representatives of the poetry subsection of Massolit, that is, Pavianov, Bogokhulsky, Sladky, Shpichkin and Adelfina Buzdyak; dancing were young men of unknown profession, with crew cuts and cotton-padded shoulders; dancing was a very elderly man with a beard in which a bit of green onion had got stuck, and dancing with him was a sickly girl, being eaten up by anemia, in a crumpled little orange silk dress.

Streaming with sweat, the waiters carried sweating mugs of beer above their heads, shouting hoarsely and with hatred: “Excuse me, citizen!” Somewhere through a megaphone a voice was commanding: “Kars shashlik, one! Zubrik, two! Tripe hospodar-style!!” The thin voice was no longer singing but howling: “Hallelujah!” The crash of the golden cymbals in the jazz band was sometimes drowned by the crash of dishes, which the dishwashers were sending down an inclined chute into the kitchen. In a word, hell.

And at midnight there was an apparition in hell. Onto the veranda came a black-eyed handsome man with a dagger-shaped beard, in tails, and cast a regal gaze over his domain. It was said, the mystics said, that there was a time when the handsome man did not wear tails but was girded with a broad leather belt with pistol butts sticking out of it, and his raven-black hair was tied up in scarlet silk, and under his command a brig sailed the Caribbean Sea under a black coffin flag with a death’s-head.

But no, no! The mystics, those seducers, lie; there are no Caribbean Seas in the world, and no desperate freebooters sail them, and no corvette gives chase, no cannon smoke drifts over the waves. There is nothing, and there never was anything! There is a sickly linden over there, there is a wrought-iron railing, and beyond it the boulevard... And the ice is melting in the little bowl, and at the next table someone’s bloodshot, bull-like eyes can be seen, and it is frightening, frightening... O gods, my gods, poison, give me poison!..

And suddenly at a table a word fluttered up: “Berlioz!!” Suddenly the jazz fell apart and went silent, as though someone had banged it with a fist. “What, what, what, what?!!” “Berlioz!!!” And they started jumping up, started crying out...

Yes, a wave of grief surged up at the terrible news about Mikhail Alexandrovich. Someone was bustling about, shouting that it was necessary right now, right here, on the spot, to draw up some sort of collective telegram and send it off at once.

But what telegram, we may ask, and where to? And why send it? Indeed, where to? And what use is any telegram whatever to him whose flattened skull is now being squeezed in the prosector’s rubber hands, whose neck is now being pierced by the professor’s curved needles? He has perished, and he needs no telegram. It is all over; let us not overload the telegraph any further.
Yes, he has perished, perished... But we, after all, are alive!

Yes, a wave of grief surged up, but it held, held, and began to subside, and here and there someone had already gone back to his table and—at first on the sly, then openly—drunk a little vodka and had a bite. Really, should the chicken cutlets de volaille go to waste? How will we help Mikhail Alexandrovich? By staying hungry? Why, we are alive, after all!

Naturally, the piano was locked, the jazz band dispersed, a few journalists left for their offices to write obituaries. It became known that Zheldybin had arrived from the morgue. He installed himself in the late man’s office upstairs, and at once a rumor rolled through that it was he who would replace Berlioz. Zheldybin summoned all twelve board members from the restaurant, and at the meeting urgently begun in Berlioz’s office they proceeded to discuss the pressing questions of decorating the columned hall of Griboyedov’s, of transferring the body from the morgue to that hall, of opening it to the public, and other matters connected with the sad event.

And the restaurant went on living its usual nighttime life, and would have gone on living it until closing, that is, until four in the morning, had something not happened that was by now quite out of the ordinary and that struck the restaurant’s guests far more than the news of Berlioz’s death.
The first to grow agitated were the cabbies on duty at the gates of the Griboyedov house. One of them could be heard, half rising on his box, shouting:
“Whoa! Just look at that!”

Following this, from out of nowhere, a little light flared up by the wrought-iron railing and began to approach the veranda. Those sitting at the tables began to rise and peer, and saw that a white ghost was proceeding toward the restaurant together with the little light. When it came right up to the trellis, everyone sat as if petrified at their tables, with bits of sterlet on their forks and their eyes popping. The doorman, who had come out of the restaurant’s cloakroom door into the courtyard at that moment for a smoke, stamped out his cigarette and started toward the ghost with the clear aim of barring its way into the restaurant, but for some reason did not do so and stopped, smiling foolishly.

And the ghost, passing through the opening in the trellis, stepped unhindered onto the veranda. Here everyone saw that this was no ghost at all, but Ivan Nikolayevich Bezdomny, the very well-known poet.

He was barefoot, in a torn, whitish tolstovka, to which, on the chest, a paper icon with the rubbed-off image of an unknown saint was fastened with a safety pin, and in striped white long johns. In his hand Ivan Nikolayevich carried a lit wedding candle. Ivan Nikolayevich’s right cheek was freshly scratched. It is hard even to measure the depth of the silence that reigned on the veranda. One could see beer flowing onto the floor from a mug tilted to one side in the hand of one of the waiters.
The poet raised the candle above his head and said loudly:
“Hail, friends!” after which he looked under the nearest table and exclaimed miserably: “No, he’s not here!”
Two voices were heard. A bass said pitilessly:
“That’s it, then. Delirium tremens.”
And a second, a woman’s, frightened, spoke these words:
“How could the police let him go through the streets like that?”
Ivan Nikolayevich heard this and responded:

“They tried to stop me twice, in Skatertny Lane and here on the Bronnaya, but I swung over a fence and, as you see, tore my cheek!” Here Ivan Nikolayevich raised the candle and cried out: “Brethren in literature!” (His hoarse voice grew stronger and more fervent.) “Listen to me, all of you! He has appeared! Catch him at once, or he’ll do untold harm!”
“What? What? What did he say? Who has appeared?” voices came from all sides.
“The consultant!” Ivan answered. “And this consultant has just killed Misha Berlioz at Patriarch’s.”
Here people came pouring out of the inner hall onto the veranda, and a crowd closed in around Ivan’s flame.
“Excuse me, excuse me, be more precise,” a quiet and polite voice said right by Ivan Nikolayevich’s ear. “Tell us, what do you mean, killed? Who killed him?”
“A foreign consultant, a professor and a spy!” Ivan responded, looking around.
“And what is his name?” someone asked quietly in his ear.

“That’s just it, the name!” Ivan cried in anguish. “If only I knew the name! I didn’t make out the name on the visiting card... All I remember is the first letter, ‘W,’ the name begins with ‘W’! What name could that be, beginning with ‘W’?” Ivan asked himself, clutching his forehead, and suddenly began to mutter: “W, w, w... Wa... Wo... Wagner? Wagner? Weiner? Wegner? Winter?” The hair on Ivan’s head began to crawl from the strain.
“Wolf?” some woman cried out pitifully.
Ivan got angry.

“You fool!” he shouted, searching for the woman with his eyes. “What has Wolf got to do with it? Wolf isn’t to blame for anything! Wo, wo... No! I won’t remember it this way! Now look here, citizens: telephone the police at once, have them send out five motorcycles with machine guns to catch the professor. And don’t forget to tell them there are two more with him: some long checked fellow... cracked pince-nez... and a black cat, a fat one. And meanwhile I’ll search Griboyedov’s... I sense that he’s here!”

Ivan grew restless, shoved aside those around him, began waving the candle, pouring wax all over himself, and looking under the tables. Here the word was heard: “A doctor!” and someone’s kindly, fleshy face, shaven and well fed, in horn-rimmed glasses, appeared in front of Ivan.

“Comrade Bezdomny,” this face began in a jubilee-speech voice, “calm down! You are upset by the death of our beloved Mikhail Alexandrovich... no, simply Misha Berlioz. We all understand that perfectly. You need rest. Our comrades will now see you to bed, and you will forget...”
“Do you,” Ivan interrupted, baring his teeth, “understand that the professor has to be caught? And you come pestering me with your nonsense! Cretin!”
“Comrade Bezdomny, for pity’s sake,” the face replied, turning red, backing away and already regretting it had got mixed up in this business.
“No, you of all people are the one I’ll show no pity,” Ivan Nikolayevich said with quiet hatred.
A spasm distorted his face; he quickly shifted the candle from his right hand to his left, swung wide and struck the sympathetic face on the ear.

Here it dawned on them to throw themselves on Ivan—and they did. The candle went out, and the glasses that had jumped off the face were instantly trampled. Ivan let out a terrible war cry, audible, to the general scandal, even on the boulevard, and began to defend himself. Dishes rang as they fell from the tables, women screamed.
While the waiters were tying up the poet with towels, a conversation was going on in the cloakroom between the commander of the brig and the doorman.
“Did you see he was in his underpants?” the pirate asked coldly.
“But, Archibald Archibaldovich,” the doorman answered, cowering, “how can I refuse the gentleman entry, if he is a member of Massolit?”
“Did you see he was in his underpants?” the pirate repeated.
“For pity’s sake, Archibald Archibaldovich,” the doorman said, turning crimson, “what can I do? I understand myself, there are ladies sitting on the veranda...”

“The ladies have nothing to do with it, it’s all the same to the ladies,” the pirate answered, literally burning the doorman up with his eyes, “but it is not all the same to the police! A man in his underwear may proceed through the streets of Moscow in only one case, if he is going under police escort, and to only one place—the police station! And you, if you are a doorman, ought to know that on seeing such a man you must, without delaying a second, start blowing your whistle. Do you hear? Do you hear what is going on on the veranda?”
Here the frantic doorman heard a sort of whooping coming from the veranda, the smashing of dishes and women’s screams.
“Well, what am I to do with you for this?” the freebooter asked.

The skin on the doorman’s face took on a typhoid tinge, and his eyes went dead. It seemed to him that the black hair, now combed into a parting, was covered with flaming silk. The shirtfront and tails vanished, and the butt of a pistol appeared behind a leather belt. The doorman pictured himself hanged from the fore-topsail yard. With his own eyes he saw his own tongue sticking out and his lifeless head drooping onto his shoulder, and even heard the splash of a wave against the side. The doorman’s knees gave way. But here the freebooter took pity on him and dimmed his piercing gaze.

“Watch out, Nikolai! This is the last time. We wouldn’t take doormen like you in this restaurant for free. Go and get yourself a job as a church watchman.” Having said this, the commander commanded precisely, clearly, quickly: “Panteley from the bar. A policeman. A report. A car. To the psychiatric hospital.” And he added: “Whistle!”

A quarter of an hour later, an extremely astonished public, not only in the restaurant but on the boulevard itself and in the windows of the houses overlooking the restaurant garden, saw Panteley, the doorman, a policeman, a waiter and the poet Ryukhin carry out of the gates of Griboyedov’s a young man swaddled like a doll, who, dissolving in tears, kept spitting, trying to hit Ryukhin in particular, and shouting for the whole boulevard to hear:
“Swine!.. Swine!..”
The driver of a truck, with a vicious face, was starting the engine. Next to him a cabby was getting his horse worked up, slapping it on the croup with lilac reins and shouting:
“Here, take a racehorse! I’ve driven ’em to the psychiatric before!”

All around, the crowd buzzed, discussing the unprecedented incident. In a word, there was a nasty, vile, juicy, swinish scandal, which ended only when the truck carried away from the gates of Griboyedov’s the unfortunate Ivan Nikolayevich, the policeman, Panteley and Ryukhin.
